hints: Focus on the gas test first, as a pungent gas that turns red litmus blue and forms white smoke with HCl is very distinctive.
That gas is ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, which tells you T must contain the ammonium ion, $\text{NH}_4^+$, so only two options remain.
Now look at the barium chloride result and remember the acid solubility difference between a sulfate precipitate and a carbonate precipitate.
walkthrough:
**Identify the gas from heating with NaOH**

Think of this as the classic test for the ammonium ion. Warming any ammonium salt with alkali releases ammonia gas.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Confirm ammonia with the two observations**

Ammonia is pungent, alkaline so it turns damp red litmus blue, and it reacts with HCl gas to make solid ammonium chloride smoke.

Confirmation reaction:
$$\text{NH}_3(g) + \text{HCl}(g) \rightarrow \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s)$$ 
This proves T contains $\text{NH}_4^+$. So T is either ammonium carbonate or ammonium sulfate.

**Identify the anion with barium chloride**

Both carbonate and sulfate give a white precipitate with $\text{BaCl}_2$, but they behave differently in acid. Barium sulfate is insoluble in dilute HCl, while barium carbonate dissolves.

Precipitate reactions:
$$\text{Ba}^{2+} + \text{SO}_4^{2-} \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s) \text{ (insoluble in HCl) }$$
$$\text{Ba}^{2+} + \text{CO}_3^{2-} \rightarrow \text{BaCO}_3(s) \text{ (dissolves in HCl) }$$
Since the precipitate did not dissolve, the anion must be sulfate. Combining $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ gives ammonium sulfate.

options.A: Ammonium carbonate would pass the first test by releasing $\text{NH}_3$, but it fails the second test. It would give white $\text{BaCO}_3$ which dissolves in dilute HCl to give $\text{BaCl}_2$, water and $\text{CO}_2$, so the precipitate would disappear.
options.B: Ammonium sulfate contains $\text{NH}_4^+$ which releases $\text{NH}_3$ on warming with NaOH, and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ which gives white $\text{BaSO}_4$ that is insoluble in dilute HCl. It matches both observations perfectly.
options.C: Sodium carbonate contains no ammonium ion, so warming with NaOH would produce no ammonia gas. It would also give $\text{BaCO}_3$ which dissolves in dilute HCl, so both tests fail.
options.D: Sodium sulfate would pass the barium chloride test by forming insoluble $\text{BaSO}_4$, but it contains $\text{Na}^+$ not $\text{NH}_4^+$. Warming with NaOH would give no gas, so the first observation rules it out.
